questions.why: It needs 2ⁿ ≥ 360 / 0.1 = 3600 positions. 2¹¹ = 2048 gives only 0.176°, while 2¹² = 4096 gives 0.088°, so 12 tracks are needed. 10 tracks (1024 positions) give 0.35°, the slide's example.
questions.ref: Slide 19 · Tracks needed for a resolution

questions.text: An 11-track absolute encoder is compared with a 600-slot incremental encoder decoded in quadruple mode. Which has the finer resolution?
options: The absolute one: about 0.18° against only 0.6°
The absolute one: about 0.088° against 0.15°
The incremental one: 0.15° against about 0.18°
The absolute one: about 0.18° against only 0.3°
questions.why: Absolute: 2¹¹ = 2048 positions, 360° / 2048 ≈ 0.176°. Incremental: 4 × 600 = 2400 counts, 360° / 2400 = 0.15°, so the incremental encoder is slightly finer. Forgetting the ×4 gives 0.6°, double counting gives 0.3°, and using 2¹² gives 0.088°.
questions.ref: Book p. 124 · Absolute versus incremental resolution

questions.text: Why do absolute encoder discs generally use Gray code rather than ordinary binary?
options: Only one bit changes between adjacent positions, so a misread at a boundary costs one count at most
It doubles the number of positions that a given number of tracks can tell apart, giving finer resolution
Its code word simply increases by one at every step, so the controller needs no decoding
It needs fewer tracks than binary for the same number of positions, so the disc can be made smaller
questions.why: Going from 0111 to 1000 in plain binary flips all four bits, and because the detectors never switch at exactly the same moment, a passing reading such as 1111 (about half a turn away) can appear. Gray code flips a single bit between neighbouring positions, so a misread is off by one count at most. It needs the same number of tracks as binary and gives the same number of positions.
questions.ref: Book p. 124 · Why Gray code is used

questions.text: The slide's Gray-code sequence for 0 to 10 is 0000, 0001, 0011, 0010, 0110, 0111, 0101, 0100, 1100, 1101, 1111. What is the 4-bit Gray code for decimal 12?
questions.why: Gray = binary XOR (binary shifted right by one bit): 1100 XOR 0110 = 1010. Continuing the reflected sequence also gives 11 → 1110 and 12 → 1010. 1100 is plain binary, 0110 is only the shifted value, and 1110 is the code for 11.

questions.text: A vertical robot axis holding a load must resume work right after a power failure without first moving to find its position. Which encoder suits it?
options: An incremental encoder with a Z channel, since its index pulse restores the position at once
A single-channel incremental encoder, since it needs only one input and no direction data
An absolute encoder, whose code word gives the position as soon as power returns
A two-channel incremental encoder in quadruple mode, since it has the finest resolution
questions.why: An absolute encoder keeps a record of its position through a power outage, so motion can resume without rehoming. An incremental encoder loses its count, and even with a Z channel it must move until the index pulse is found, which is risky for a loaded axis that stopped part-way through a cycle.
questions.ref: Slide 20 · Absolute encoder after power loss

questions.text: How does a sonar sensor measure the distance to an obstacle?
options: It emits a pulsed 40 kHz infrared beam and measures the angle of the reflected spot
It emits a short burst at 50–250 kHz and measures the time until the echo returns
It emits a burst of about 1 s at 20–200 Hz and measures how loud the returning echo is
It emits a laser pulse and compares the phase of the returning light with a reference
questions.why: A short acoustic signal (about 1 ms, ultrasonic, 50–250 kHz) is emitted and the time until the echo returns is measured. This time of flight is proportional to twice the distance of the nearest obstacle in the cone. Measurements repeat about 20 times per second, giving the typical clicking sound.

questions.text: A sonar echo returns 8.75 ms after the pulse is emitted. Taking the speed of sound as 343 m/s, how far away is the obstacle?
questions.why: The pulse goes out and back, so d = v·t / 2 = 343 × 0.00875 / 2 ≈ 1.50 m. 3.00 m forgets the factor of two, 0.75 m halves twice, and 15.01 m comes from writing 8.75 ms as 0.0875 s.
questions.ref: Book p. 126 · Sonar time of flight

questions.text: A sonar repeats its measurement 25 times per second, and each echo must return before the next pulse. What is the maximum range it can measure unambiguously (sound at 343 m/s)?
questions.why: At 25 Hz there are 40 ms between pulses. Sound covers 343 × 0.04 = 13.72 m in that time, out and back, so the maximum range is 13.72 / 2 = 6.86 m. 13.72 m forgets the round trip, 8.58 m is the result for 20 measurements per second (50 ms), and 3.43 m halves the result again.
questions.ref: Book p. 126 · Repetition rate and range

questions.text: On a robot with a ring of 24 sonars, what does interference between the sensors typically cause, and what prevents it?
options: Obstacles appear further away than they really are; coded (pseudo-random) signals prevent it
Obstacles appear closer than they really are; coded (pseudo-random) signals prevent it
Obstacles appear further away than they really are; raising the frequency to 250 kHz prevents it
Obstacles are not detected at all; firing all 24 sensors at the same instant prevents it
questions.why: Interference happens when one sensor picks up another sensor's signal and so assumes an obstacle closer than the real one. Coded sonar signals, for example pseudo-random codes, let each sensor accept only its own echo. An obstacle seeming further away is the angled-reflection problem, and firing all sensors at once causes crosstalk.

questions.text: A sonar beam meets a smooth wall at an incident angle larger than the critical angle. What is the most likely result?
options: The wall absorbs most of the ultrasound, so the echo returns weak but at the right range
The echo is scattered evenly in all directions, so the reading is reliable at any angle
The echo comes straight back, but the wall appears slightly closer than it really is
The echo is reflected away as if by a mirror, so the wall may not be detected at all
questions.why: Smooth surfaces behave like mirrors: beyond a critical angle, which depends on the operating frequency and the reflective material, no detectable echo returns, so a plane or a corner goes unseen (Fig. a, b). In complex surroundings, such mirror reflections can also bounce via other surfaces and produce a false, virtual object (Fig. c).
questions.ref: Slide 27 · Smooth surfaces and the critical angle

questions.text: Which method is named as the most accurate way to measure changes in distance (rather than absolute distance) with a laser?
options: Interferometry
Light-wave phase shift
Triangulation with a detector array
Pulse time of flight
questions.why: The most common laser rangefinder uses time of flight, and measuring the phase shift against a reference signal is another option; interferometry is the most accurate for changes in distance. It tracks fringes relative to wherever it started, so on its own it cannot give an absolute distance.

questions.text: A laser rangefinder's pulse returns 80 ns after it was sent. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, how far away is the target?
options: 6 m
questions.why: d = c·t / 2 = 3 × 10⁸ × 80 × 10⁻⁹ / 2 = 12 m. 24 m forgets that the pulse travels out and back, and 6 m halves twice. In 1 ns light moves only about 30 cm, which is why laser ranging needs such precise timing.

questions.text: An autonomous vehicle needs a 3-D point cloud of its surroundings. Which description fits the sensor it would use?
options: A single laser rangefinder, since it measures many objects at the same time
A ring of 24 sonars of about 15° each, all fired at the same time
A LiDAR: a laser scanner with an extra rotating degree of freedom
An infrared triangulation sensor fitted with a longer detector array
questions.why: A laser rangefinder measures the distance to one object at a time, so it is a one-dimensional sensor. Using another degree of freedom at the rotating assembly lets a 3-D scanner collect 3-D point cloud data; such scanners are called LiDAR and are often used on autonomous vehicles.

questions.text: Why do infrared distance sensors not work on the time-of-flight principle like sonar?
options: A photon's flight time is far too short to measure with a simple, cheap circuit
Infrared light is absorbed by the air, so the reflected beam never reaches the sensor
The speed of light changes with air temperature far more than that of sound, so the timing would drift
An infrared LED cannot be pulsed, so there is no start time to measure from
questions.why: Light is so fast that its time of flight would be much too short for a simple and cheap sensor arrangement. IR sensors instead use a pulsed infrared LED (about 40 kHz) with a detection array and find the distance from the angle of the reflected beam.
questions.ref: Slide 33 · Why IR does not use time of flight

questions.text: An infrared distance sensor with a pulsed LED and a detector array works out the range from ......
options: the angle of the reflected beam, i.e. where its spot lands on the array
the time between sending the 40 kHz pulse and receiving its reflected echo
the intensity of the reflected light, which falls off as the distance grows
the phase shift between the reflected light and a reference signal
questions.why: The angle under which the reflected beam is received changes with the distance to the object, so the spot's position on the array measures the range (triangulation across the emitter–detector baseline). The range is worked out from where the spot lands, not from how bright the returned light is.

questions.text: The beam of an infrared distance sensor is invisible to the eye. How can you check that the emitter is actually working?
options: Lower the pulse rate from 40 kHz until the beam can be seen flickering by eye
Reflect it off a plain mirror, which shifts the infrared light into the visible range
View it with an IR detector card or an IR-sensitive camera, such as a phone camera
Raise the LED current until the infrared beam glows as a visible red light
questions.why: The wavelength is invisible, but it can be made visible with IR detector cards or by recording the beam with an IR-sensitive camera. Most phone cameras block infrared only partly, so a working emitter shows up on the screen as a glowing spot.

questions.text: A 1000-slot encoder decoded in quadruple mode is sampled every 1 ms, and velocity is found by differencing successive positions. What velocity error does a single-count error cause?
questions.why: One count is 360° / 4000 = 0.09°, and dividing by Δt = 0.001 s gives 0.09 / 0.001 = 90°/s (15 rpm). 0.09°/s forgets to divide by Δt, and 360°/s forgets the ×4. This amplification of noise by numerical differentiation is why tachometers are used to measure velocity directly.

questions.text: What is the main drawback of the DC tachometers commonly used in robotics, compared with AC tachometers?
options: Their output voltage is proportional to the joint angle, so it must still be differentiated
Their permanent-magnet field weakens as speed rises, so the output becomes non-linear
Their commutators add a slight ripple to the output voltage that cannot be fully filtered
They need a separate field supply, which makes them larger than AC tachometers
questions.why: A DC tachometer is a DC generator whose field comes from permanent magnets; because the field is constant, the output voltage is proportional to angular velocity. Its commutators cause a slight ripple that cannot be entirely filtered out, which AC tachometers avoid, though the simpler DC type is the one generally used in robotics.

questions.text: A DC tachometer has a constant of 0.05 V per rad/s, and its output reads 6 V. What is the shaft speed?
options: 120 rpm
7200 rpm
1146 rpm
questions.why: The output is proportional to angular velocity, so ω = V / K = 6 / 0.05 = 120 rad/s, and 120 × 60 / (2π) ≈ 1146 rpm. 120 rpm leaves the answer in rad/s, 7200 rpm multiplies by 60 without dividing by 2π, and 0.0796 rpm comes from dividing K by V instead of V by K.

questions.text: Tactile sensors fitted in a robot's fingers improve its manipulation. What information do they provide?
options: The angular position of each finger joint, just as an encoder would give it
The distribution of contact force between the finger and the object
The temperature of the object, so that hot parts are never grasped
The speed at which each finger closes, as a tachometer would give
questions.why: In robotic fingers, a tactile array gives the contact force distribution between the finger and the manipulated object. A distribution says more than a single force: whether the object is centred, slipping or held at an angle.

questions.text: Why is an array of tactile sensors sometimes used as an artificial skin over a robot's body?
options: To measure the distance to obstacles several metres away, as a ring of sonars does
To measure the joint velocities directly, so that no tachometer has to be fitted
To sense contact with objects or people, making it safer to work beside humans
To pad the arm against impacts, acting only as a soft protective layer
questions.why: To increase safety, for example when working with a human, tactile sensors can form an artificial skin that lets the robot sense contacts with objects in its environment and stop or yield. Tactile sensing is based on an array of touch sensors.

questions.text: Which pairing of tactile sensing principle and how it works is correct?
options: Capacitive: the force changes the distance between the plates or their area
Magnetic: strain gauges connected in a Wheatstone bridge measure the surface strain
Optical: the change in magnetic flux density is measured as the compliant layer moves
Mechanical: the received light intensity varies with the displacement
questions.why: In a capacitive element, the force changes the plate spacing or area and so the capacitance. Strain gauges in a Wheatstone bridge belong to deformation-based sensors (not magnetic ones), flux-density changes to magnetic sensors and light intensity to optical sensors; mechanical sensors are on/off micro-switches.
